title: The attack on Pearl Harbor, 7 December 1941

clock.name: Hawaiian time

others.name: Tokyo time (the Japanese records, on the Tokyo date, 8 December)
others.rule: subtract 19 h 30 min (add 4 h 30 min and take a day off): 03:25 JST 8 Dec = 07:55 HST 7 Dec

others.name: GCT (the Bishop’s Point radio log; Monaghan’s despatch)

clock.note: Hawaii kept UTC−10:30 until war time began on 9 February 1942 (tz database, citing Schmitt and Cox 1992). The Japanese records keep Tokyo time and the Tokyo date. The ships’ own clocks were set by hand and remembered: CINCPAC found “great conflicts in these reports”.

cloud.note: cumulus mostly over the mountains, more after eight with lower cloud over the harbour at times (CINCPAC); a dense layer north of the island that the first wave flew over

sun.note: computed (R10 §11.5): 17° high at 123–124° over Battleship Row at 07:57, low behind the torpedo planes

weather.note: Partly cloudy, a light northerly breeze and smooth water in the harbour. From about ten past eight thick smoke from Arizona and the airfields lay over Battleship Row and hampered the guns.

japan.name: Imperial Japanese Navy: the First Air Fleet (Kidō Butai) and the midget submarines

usa.name: United States Pacific Fleet, the Hawaiian Air Force and the Marines at ʻEwa

events.text: Ward sights a submarine’s conning tower trailing Antares toward the harbour entrance.

tellings.says: “WE HAVE ATTACKED FIRED UPON AND DROPPED DEPTH CHARGES UPON SUBMARINE OPERATING IN DEFENSIVE SEA AREA” (1723 GCT).

stops.text: 06:40, Hawaiian time. Off the harbour entrance the destroyer Ward attacks a midget submarine following a supply ship in. Her report reaches the naval district within the half hour.
07:02. At Opana, on Oʻahu’s north point, a radar left on for training shows a large formation far to the north. The report is taken for the B-17s expected from California.
07:40. North of Kahuku the first wave deploys: torpedo and level bombers swing west along the north shore, dive bombers and fighters cut down the middle of the island.
07:55. Dive bombers hit Wheeler, Hickam and Ford Island’s hangars as the colours are being hoisted on the ships. Torpedo planes come in low from the south-east toward Battleship Row.
07:58. Helm, the one ship under way, fights the torpedo planes crossing the channel with her after guns and makes for the entrance.
08:06. A bomb from the level bombers strikes Arizona forward; her forward magazines explode.

tellings.says: 1,177 of her crew lost their lives.

stops.text: 08:10. Oklahoma has rolled over at her berth with men trapped inside her. Across Ford Island, Utah is going over too. Smoke from Arizona covers the row.
08:33. A pair of Army fighter pilots who took off from Haleʻiwa on their own find dive bombers strafing the Marine field at ʻEwa.
08:40. Nevada gets under way without tugs and backs clear of the burning Arizona; the second wave is sighting the island. Inside the harbour, Monaghan rams a midget submarine.
08:52. The second wave’s dive bombers find a battleship under way in the channel and go for her.
09:06. Bombs fall on Drydock No. 1: Pennsylvania is hit, and the destroyers ahead of her in the dock burn.
09:10. Nevada is run aground at the turn off Hospital Point, clear of the channel, rather than sink in it.
09:30. Shaw’s forward magazine explodes in the floating dock. The last attackers are leaving for the rendezvous off Kaʻena Point.
09:45. The last Japanese aircraft have gone. The fires burn on along Battleship Row, at the airfields and in the dock.

moments.title: Kaga’s torpedo unit comes in low over the Southeast Loch

role.name: a Type 97 carrier attack aircraft of Kaga’s torpedo unit

objective.text: Put your torpedo into an outboard battleship.

beats.text: The first torpedoes are in the water.
Machine guns open from the battleships and the Navy Yard.
Across Ford Island, torpedo planes come in on the ships moored on its far side.

checkpoints.text: Your torpedo is away; get out low over the harbour.

record.note: which carrier’s torpedoes struck which ship is not settled; the box keeps Oklahoma’s with Akagi’s unit

after.text: Kaga’s torpedo unit came in low over the Southeast Loch and released at the outboard battleships. West Virginia was torn open along her side and settled upright on the bottom; Oklahoma, ahead of her, rolled over within minutes with men trapped inside her. Kaga’s torpedo unit lost more aircraft than any other that morning; their crews did not return.

tellings.says: West Virginia: seven torpedoes and two dud bombs. Oklahoma: about five torpedoes and three near misses.
Oklahoma: 429 lost their lives. West Virginia: 106.
Five of Kaga’s twelve torpedo bombers were lost.

objective.text: Take Nevada clear of the burning ships and down the channel; keep her guns firing; do not let her sink in the channel.

beats.text: Vestal is towed clear of Arizona.
The second wave is over the island.
Dive bombers come at you from the south-west.
Bombs fall on the drydock: Pennsylvania, Cassin and Downes are hit.

checkpoints.text: The turn off Hospital Point is ahead.

track: off 1010 Dock and Drydock No. 1 about 08:55
aground at the turn off Hospital Point about 09:10
record.note: her record answer was to beach her at the turn so that she could not sink in the channel

after.text: Nevada got under way alone, her bow already torn by a torpedo, and steamed down the channel past the burning battleships while the second wave’s dive bombers concentrated on her. Hit again and again and down by the head, she was run aground at the turn off Hospital Point so that she could not sink in the channel and block it. She was refloated and repaired, and fought again, off Normandy among other places.

tellings.says: One torpedo and five bombs.
60 killed and 109 wounded (DANFS, verify).

moments.title: Dive bombers find a battleship under way

role.name: a Type 99 carrier bomber of Kaga’s dive-bombing unit

objective.text: Hit the battleship moving down the channel.

beats.text: Every gun in the harbour is firing now.
The second wave’s attack order: all units attack.

checkpoints.text: Your bomb is away; pull out low over the water.

record.note: the record has her beached at the turn, not sunk in the channel

after.text: Kaga’s dive bombers found a battleship under way in the channel and went for her, hoping to sink her where she would block the harbour. She was hit repeatedly but was beached at the turn off Hospital Point, and the channel stayed open. Kaga lost more dive bombers than any other carrier that morning; their crews did not return.

tellings.says: The second wave lost 14 dive bombers (answer 40).
Kaga lost six D3As.

role.name: a P-40B of the 47th Pursuit Squadron

objective.text: Break up the line of dive bombers strafing the Marine field at ʻEwa.

beats.text: Dive bombers are strafing ʻEwa from just above the trees.

checkpoints.text: Your ammunition is running low; Wheeler is to the north.

record.note: claims, never losses: the Japanese records list one dive bomber of the first wave lost, Shōkaku’s

after.text: A pair of Army fighter pilots, whose squadron had been sent to Haleʻiwa for gunnery practice, took off on their own and found Japanese dive bombers strafing the Marine field at ʻEwa. They claimed several; the Japanese records list one dive bomber of the first wave lost. They landed at Wheeler, rearmed and went up again into the second wave.

tellings.says: “Each getting two confirmed kills during this first engagement”; the Army’s claims for the day were 10 confirmed and 4 probables.
The Japanese lost 29 aircraft to all causes (answer 40).

moments.title: Helm, the one ship under way

objective.text: Get to sea, fight the aircraft over the channel, and find the submarine off the entrance.

beats.text: Torpedo planes cross the West Loch channel ahead of you, strafing.
A conning tower to the right of the channel, north of the first buoy.
The steering motor shorts: steer by engines.

checkpoints.text: You are at sea; the submarine has gone down.

record.note: her claim of an aircraft at 08:10 is a claim

after.text: Helm, the one ship under way when the attack began, fought the torpedo planes crossing the channel with her after guns and made for the entrance. Off the reef she fired on a midget submarine’s conning tower and missed; then her steering failed and she steered by her engines. A near miss later damaged her lightly. The midget she fired on is usually identified with the one that grounded on the windward coast the next day; its commander was taken prisoner.

tellings.says: 90 rounds of 5-inch and 350 of .50 calibre in the day.
2,390 Americans lost their lives: 2,341 service members and 49 civilians, “some due to enemy actions and others from friendly fire”.
2,403, with 68 civilians (Conn et al. 2000).
The Japanese lost 29 aircraft; the airmen and the midget submarines’ crews killed are given as 64, one taken prisoner (Wikipedia, tertiary).
